newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Investors in Lithuania want legal, tax reform.
newsitem.headline: Investors in Lithuania want legal, tax reform.

text.p: The Lithuanian Investment Agency said on Friday that its annual survey of foreign businesses operating in the Baltic state showed widespread dissatisfaction with the country's legal and tax systems.
It said 34 of 46 foreign investors responded, representing some two-thirds of estimated foreign direct investment (FDI), or $280 million out of $450 million, by end 1996.
"The legal, tax and customs systems were strongly criticised. Fundamental administrative reform is desired, especially an end to unclear and unstable rules," the agency said in a statement.
"Legal instability, a lack of transparency and the lack of a unified code of reliable rules were the most frequent complaints," it said.
It said that a perception of corruption among bureaucrats was also a serious problem.
Foreign investment is an area where Lithuania is regarded as lagging behind Baltic cousins Latvia and Estonia, despite better relations with Russia and comparative political stability.

The country's new right-of-centre government, led by Gediminas Vagnorius, says it is determined to shake off this image and attract foreign invesment flows to match those of Lithuania's northern neighbours.

The agency said most respondents, of which half also have investments in other central European states, thought Lithuania was a good place for business but rated it below neighbours Latvia and Estonia and higher than Russia and Romania.
The agency said that labour quality, labour cost and access to the East were considered to be among the comparative advantages of investing in Lithuania.
"Geographic location is considered a significant advantage, though not a major reason to invest. Many investors included Lithuania as part of a global or regional marketing strategy," it added.
But the agency said 83 percent of the respondents said they would invest in Lithuania again.
